# Where the expected results come from

One row per scenario. "Source" names the documentation page and section the expected fragment and verdicts rest
on; "Reasoning" explains verdicts worked out by hand and why the case is here.

All paths are probed under `testutil.LabProfile()` unless the scenario sets a profile.

| Scenario | Source | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| np-deny-all-ingress | Network Policies concept page, "Default policies", "Default deny all ingress traffic" | Every pod of `default` is ingress-isolated with no rule, so nothing reaches it, from pods, the internet or private networks. Egress is untouched: a pod of `default` reaches a namespace without policies and the internet. |
| np-allow-all-ingress | Same page, "Allow all ingress traffic" | The page states that with this policy no other policy can cause an incoming connection to be denied, so the deny-all policy beside it changes nothing: policies are additive. |
| np-deny-all-egress | Same page, "Default deny all egress traffic" | Pods of `default` open no connection anywhere, DNS included. Ingress to them and egress of other namespaces stay open. |
| np-allow-all-egress | Same page, "Allow all egress traffic" | As for ingress: the allow-all policy wins over the deny-all one beside it. |
| np-deny-all | Same page, "Default deny all ingress and all egress traffic" | Both directions of `default` are closed; two pods of another namespace stay open to each other and the internet. |
| np-docs-example | Same page, "The NetworkPolicy resource" (`test-network-policy`) and the list of what it does; Namespace `myproject` labeled `project: myproject` | The page's list: `role: db` accepts TCP 6379 from `role: frontend` pods of `default`, from any pod of a namespace labeled `project: myproject` and from 172.17.0.0/16 less 172.17.1.0/24, and opens only TCP 5978 to 10.0.0.0/24. Both Namespaces are declared so that their labels are known. `external-private` holds addresses inside and outside each ipBlock, so those paths are `placement`; both blocks are private, so the internet is denied. 10.0.0.0/24 and 172.17.0.0/16 lie outside the lab's pod CIDR, so no pod matches them whether or not the plugin applies ipBlock to pods. |
| np-peers-and-or | Same page, "Behavior of to and from selectors" | One element holding both selectors needs both (alice's `role: client` pods alone); two elements need either: any pod of alice, or a `role: client` pod of the policy's own namespace. bob's client is in neither. |
| np-namespace-by-name | Same page, "Targeting a Namespace by its name"; Namespaces page, "Automatic labelling" | The control plane sets `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` to the name, replacing a written value, so `frontend` matches although its manifest claims `reports`. `jobs` and `reports` have no Namespace object; the automatic label is still known, so `jobs` is allowed and `reports` denied, not unknown. |
| np-port-range | Same page, "Targeting a range of ports" (`multi-port-egress`) | TCP 32000-32768 to 10.0.0.0/24 only. The block is part of `external-private`, so inside the range the path is `placement`; every other port, UDP, the internet and other pods are denied. |
| np-named-port | NetworkPolicy API reference, `NetworkPolicyPort.port` | A named port is resolved on each destination pod: `http` is 8080 on one workload and 8081 on another. A selected pod that declares no `http` port gets nothing from the rule. The rule has no `from`, so the internet reaches 8080 too. |
| np-api-defaults | NetworkPolicy API reference: `policyTypes` defaults to Ingress, plus Egress when egress rules exist; `protocol` defaults to TCP | `api` writes egress rules, so it is isolated both ways; `db` writes none, so its egress stays open. Ports without a protocol allow TCP and not UDP. |
| np-sctp-only-rule | Network Policies concept page, "SCTP support" | The only rule allows SCTP, which the model leaves out. The pod stays isolated: the rule must not turn into a rule for every port. |
| np-ipv6-only-peer | Same page, "Behavior of to and from selectors", ipBlock | The only peer of each rule is IPv6, which matches no IPv4 connection. The rules are dropped, the pod stays isolated both ways: neither becomes a rule for every peer. |
| np-mixed-rule | Same page, "The NetworkPolicy resource": a rule allows traffic that matches both its `from` and its `ports` | The IPv6 peer and the SCTP port are dropped from a rule that keeps an IPv4-capable peer and TCP and UDP ports: the client reaches TCP 80 and UDP 53, nothing else, and nobody else gets in. |
| svc-mapping | Service concept page: "Defining a Service" (`my-service`, 80 to 9376), "Port definitions" (`nginx-service`, named `http-web-svc`), "Multi-port Services", "Services without selectors", "Service type" (ExternalName, LoadBalancer) | A Service is a transform and allows or blocks nothing. Policies and paths are about container ports, so the allow of tcp/9376 opens 9376 and not the Service port 80 or the other target 9377. A Service with no selector or of type ExternalName selects no pods. The AWS Load Balancer Controller acts on the LoadBalancer's pods, so the internet's path to them is unknown (`aws-controller-effect`). A path to the bare Pod is unknown (`standalone-pod`). |
| workloads | Deployment, CronJob and Pod concept page examples (`nginx-deployment`, `hello`, `nginx`); Pod Security Standards on host namespaces and host ports | Each controller's pod template becomes one workload. An allow-all ingress policy gives every pod a NetworkPolicy step: plain workloads stay open, the host-network one is unknown because NetworkPolicy does not hold for it as written, the bare Pod is unknown (`standalone-pod`). A hostPort does not change the in-cluster path to the pod. |
| kinds | `model.UnsupportedKinds` and `model.IgnoredKinds`, which name each kind's reason; reason scopes in `model/reason.go` | Namespaced Calico and Cilium policies make the Kubernetes steps of their namespace's pods undetermined, in both directions. A Rollout's pod template makes every path with an end in its namespace unknown. Certificate is only a warning, ConfigMap and Secret nothing, so `app` stays open. Ingress, TargetGroupBinding, SecurityGroupPolicy and ENIConfig act on AWS steps or paths the lab does not have or that cannot be named, so no probe rests on them. Cluster-scoped policy kinds are left out, since one would make every path unknown. |
| expectations | `model.ExpectationsFile` (format and rejected entries) and `model.ExpectationStatus` (status rule) | `web-reaches-payments` is judged on the Service's target port 8080, which the policy allows from `web`: satisfied. 9090 is not allowed: violated. `web` has no egress policy, so the internet is reached: satisfied. `orders-db` picks nothing in an environment without AWS, and port 81 is not a port of the Service: both unverifiable. The three rejected entries use protocol `all`, name a Service as source, and have no side of the application's own. |
| cluster-namespaces | Network Policies concept page, "Targeting multiple namespaces by label"; `model.Namespace` on where labels come from | No git source declares a namespace, so labels come from the cluster read: `analytics` matches `team: analytics`, `marketing` does not. `sandbox` is in neither, so whether it matches is unknown (`namespace-labels-unknown`). The internet is no namespace's pod and is denied. |
| np-invalid | Kubernetes API concepts, "Field validation": under strict validation an unknown field rejects the object | The policy misspells `ingress`, so it is never applied and what `shop` allows after deployment cannot be told. `object-invalid` is input level with namespace scope: every path with an end in `shop` is unknown; paths within `other` are unaffected. |
